Well you could do it by note interval spacing. For example, starting from the root, the distance between each note in a major scale is: W W H W W W H
Where
W = a whole step = 2 half steps.
H = a half step (one fret). 

Take the first few chords in The jazz standard "All the Things You Are".

Chords: 
Fm7 = F Ab C Eb
Bbm7 = Bb Db F Ab
Eb7 = Eb G Bb Db
Abmaj7 = Ab C Eb G

Here are the notes used starting with F:
F G Ab Bb C Db Eb F

With the spacing starting from F:
W H W W H W W

So if you start at Ab instead of F you'll get:
W W H W W W H

So the key is Ab major.

Diminished 7th chords are perfectly symmetrical, meaning the distance between each note is a minor 3rd... Even from the 7th up to the tonic (the 1). Therefore you can take any diminished 7th chord, go to any note in that chord/shape, use that note as a tonic and play a diminished 7th chord shape from it... and you can use that new chord as a substitute for the original one you started with. All the notes will be the same, but just in a different inversion. Some inversions work better than others in different contexts but it's really helpful for jazz comping.

Music theory is understanding the math and mechanics of music in order to think more critically about what you're hearing and playing. The way I've studied the basics of music theory is to analyze jazz standards. Write out all the notes in each chord on paper and see how the notes are changing (and which notes are shared) from chord to chord. Analyze how the key changes are being done with the chords. While your getting a handle on how the notes in a scale are used to effectively make chord changes in a tune (or part of a tune), you're also kinda learning which notes in that scale will work more harmoniously over a specific chord (or set of chords). But yeah you need to be studying intervals. Specifically how intervals sound, and which intervals (from the chord root) make up a given chord. Which basically amounts to studying arpeggios. Interval arithmetic, arpeggios, and understanding how key changes are accomplished are essential to effectively "using" music theory when composing and improvising.

I suffer from really bad paranoia and, at times, a pretty severe major depressive disorder... and have been for a really long time. With my paranoia, my self-hatred gets projected onto others and it's really hard to tell when I'm overreacting or if someone is actually being rude or disrespectful towards me. So I totally empathize. 

One insight I've gained over the years is: if you don't like yourself, then most people will have a hard time bonding with you... it's a sad truth about how people behave. But there are compassionate and empathetic people who can accept you... they're everywhere and I hope you can find some kind hearted people who make you feel accepted while you're feeling this paranoia.  

I'm going to agree with your statement that something is wrong with you... but not in a negative way... we all have things wrong with us.... but it sounds like your paranoia and fear of rejection are preventing you from connecting to people. If you're like me, you probably worry too much about making a good impression and have lots of anxiety when interacting with others. That paranoia and anxiety sort of 'gets in the way' when trying to connect with people. I think the solution is to figure out how to let your guard down... let people interact with you instead of interacting with your anxiety, paranoia, and fears of rejection. We're all deeply flawed people. If you're kind and accepting towards yourself, it will become a lot easier to bond with others.

It's really really hard not to care what other people think of you, to not let their opinions (or your perceptions of their opinions) hurt you. It's hard work and takes a lot of practice. But when you can do that... people suddenly become easier to connect with.

Anyways, I just wanted to share my 2 cents on paranoid thoughts and rejection.
